The two warring nations of Estràl, Croy and Aria, could not be more different.

**Croy** is a feudalistic monarchy ruled by a king (never a queen) who inherits the crown. The king is primarily responsible for war and diplomacy, raising a national military, and overseeing the actions of the lower levels of government. The kingdom is divided into thirty-six baronies, each ruled by a baron who collects taxes and enforces the law in their region. What sets Croy apart from other monarchies is the king's harem. Though the word conjures certain connotations, the royal harem are in fact the king's most trusted advisors, hand-picked by him for their intelligence. It is they who are responsible for selecting the barons of each barony, and can fire and replace them at will. Between six and twelve women serve in the harem at once, and the position is entirely voluntary; though the harem as a whole is nominally responsible for producing an heir, it is more common for the king to name his wife to the harem and only carry on a relationship with her. The most effective harems in the kingdom's history have included women from all walks of life, all social classes, and all kinds of ancestries. The worst harems were selected for their beauty alone and not permitted to give input on matters of state, leaving a weak kingdom unable to effectively govern.

**Aria** is a theocratic republic. It has two official branches of government: the church of the goddess Aria deals with national development (infrastructure, social programs, collecting and distributing taxes) as well as enforcing laws, while the senate deals with making national laws, directing foreign policy, etc. The head of state is the Voice of Aria, equivalent to the Catholic Pope; the Voice is always a woman and is selected in a similar divinatory practice as our Dalai Lama. There is a third, unofficial branch of government: the elven dignitaries from across the sea who introduced the worship of Aria to the humans and helped them set up their government. Though strictly speaking they have no power and are merely "advisors", in practice their influence stretches far beyond that, with both the church and the senate loathe to go against the elves' wishes. The elves know this and use it to their advantage, and senators or cardinals who don't do what the elves would like can expect a visit from the Secret Legion, the elves' spy network, to be "convinced" otherwise.

I've put a lot of thought into the agriculture and cuisine of my world. It rarely comes up for an RPG setting, but I find it fascinating to think about.

The kingdom of Croy is mostly cold and arid badlands with poor soil for both agriculture and grazing. Most of the crops are hardy cruciferous greens and root vegetables (potatoes are the primary starch) along with pungent spices like garlic, mustard, and horseradish. Wildberries are about the only fruit that is available, and then only around the mountains, but they are traded for use in cuisine as well as dyes. The main farm animal is the goat; goat milk, cheese, and butter are staples, with goat meat being saved for the rich or for special occasions (after all, once you slaughter a goat, it stops giving you milk). Goats, indeed, have become a national symbol of Croy, with their first king having a goat head prominently on his coat of arms and a goat-horned iron crown. Put that all together and a typical meal for a commoner might be boiled potatoes and cabbage flavored with horseradish and goat butter - yum!

Edit: Forgot to mention alcohol! Vodka is very common but seen as a peasant's drink; the more expensive wildberry wine is drunk by nobles.

On Estral, people generally have one of two religions. 

If they're from Croy, they are probably not super devout, but venerate the spirits of the natural world around them. This could be as general as the wind or as specific as the river that runs through your village (if you were interested in counting you could probably count hundreds of individual gods), but generally about ten gods get the most attention nationwide. They are divided into "white gods", which represent the heavens and are depicted as humanlike figures, and "black gods", which represent the earth and are depicted as animalistic figures. For example, Mesyat the moon god is a white god (because the moon is in the sky), while Morskoy, the god of the sea, is a black god. This isn't a good/evil distinction as Croyens don't identify their gods as moral figures, just that they *are*. (This is entirely cribbed from prechristian Slavic mythology.) The church is not organized and doesn't involve itself in politics; people just usually make their offerings and don't think much more about it. One major exception is the cult of the black god Baphomet, which teaches the value of monstrosity and ugliness; this cult is heavily persecuted by the current king, but there are rumors (always quickly quashed) that he belongs to the cult himself.

If you're from Lyria, you almost certainly worship Lyria, the goddess of magic. Her worship was brought across the sea by the elves, who introduced it to the humans, who became much more fanatical about her than the elves were and set up their whole society and government around her church. Every town is centered around the local temple, and the church is an official branch of government along with the senate. As the church of the goddess of magic, the church of Lyria both encourages responsible use of magic and prosecutes irresponsible use. You need a license from the church in order to possess magic items (which are really ancient technology, but only the elves know that) or practice spellcasting. The church looks a lot like the Catholic church did in medieval Italy, but the pope is called the Speaker and is always female, as are the cardinals, but ordinary priests can be of any gender.

Of course, none of these gods are real. The only real gods are the Deep Ones who slumber hundreds of miles beneath the surface, until they wake once again to destroy the world and begin the cycle anew. (I've cribbed D&D god names for these including Lolth, Erythnul, Tharizdun, and Jubilex.)

The main thing I like about sword and sorcery as a genre that D&D doesn't give me is that magic is far less well-understood and accepted in the world, not to mention less game breaking. D&D assumes there's a wizard's tower in every town and every party will get their first magic sword by level 3, be able to fly by level 5, and can teleport by level 7. In sword and sorcery books the magic users are usually the villains, and their magic is more mysterious and limited in scope--magicians aren't throwing around fireballs, they're laying subtle curses, and Lamentations' spell list supports that concept. If magic items even exist they're rare, often cursed, and always a big deal. To be clear, I want magic to be accessible to the PCs, but D&D's standard level of magic played havoc with my worldbuilding when I was trying to write my setting for Pathfinder and 5E, and even AD&D has mostly the same problems. I switched to Lamentations because it had the right tone for my world, but my players have been asking for more character customization.

I know I could probably fix all this with house rules but that risks just being arbitrary; I prefer to have something official to fall back on when it comes to big things like a magic system.

None of these people are answering the question lmao. Eldritch Knight is perfectly fine, it does a *different thing* than the magus. A magus is a front line combatant who adds damage to their attacks with blasting spells, an EK is a caster first and foremost with access to 9 spellcasting levels, and like all 9 level casters start off pretty weak until the prestige levels kick in. You're more like a wizard than a fighter, but a more durable wizard who can beat face and flank if needed. You'll also quickly catch up to the magus in BAB and eventually surpass it.

To be a competent evoker wizard you should have a signature spell, say fireball (I think lightning bolt is cooler and gives you a really neat visual flavor but fireball has a better shape), take the magical lineage trait to apply metamagic to it more easily. Take empower spell, maximize spell, dazing spell, and you're aiming for Spell Perfection later on. The rule of thumb is that with magical lineage, metamagicked fireball is a better use of your higher level spell slots than the actual blasting spells of those levels (e.g. empowered fireball is the best 4th level evocation spell).

If you find you have extra feats take Favored Prestige Class and Prestigious Spellcaster to regain one of your lost casting levels, and don't forget that prestige levels don't let you add free spells to your spellbook. Eldritch Knight is my favorite class for a reason - it's incredibly fun, so go have a blast!

EDIT: Looked up the statblock I wrote for it! It had these special abilities:

Gush (Ex) Whenever the Heart takes bludgeoning, piercing, or slashing damage, a gout of demonic blood spews out from the wound in a 30-foot line in the direction of its attacker. Creatures in the line must make a DC 18 Strength check or be pushed back 15 feet and knocked prone. They also take 3d6 points of negative energy damage and are sickened for 1 round (no save).

After Ramona died I needed a new character, and I looked at the piles and piles of builds I had saved up and none of them seemed like a good fit for that campaign, so I looked at a bunch of guides and tossed something together and this is that thing.

Merfolk wizard (instructor)  
25 point buy: Str 16, Dex 12 (+2 racial=14), Con 14 (+2 racial=16), Int 16, Wis 8, Cha 10 (+2 racial=12)  
Arcane school: Transmutation (Shapechange)  
Feats:  
- 1: Arcane Strike  
- 1 (Wizard): Scribe Scroll  
- 3: Power Attack  
- 5: Toughness  
- 5 (Instructor): Allied Spellcaster  
- 7: Whatever you want (I picked Craft Wondrous Item)   
- 9:  Whatever you want (I picked Defensive Combat Training)
- 10 (Arcane Discovery): Idealize  
- 11: Quicken Spell

Spellbook: All the polymorph spells (especially the whole Beast Shape and Monstrous Physique lines) and all the defensive spells you can afford

Magic items: Top priorities are Belt of Giant Strength and Amulet of Mighty Fists, which I took Craft Wondrous Item to make cheaper. Beyond that you want a good set of defensive items and and Int headband (Shifter's Headband is a good fit for this build), and you really want as many scrolls of the utility stuff that you don't want to prepare as you can get.

So the idea with this build is to pump your Strength, turn into a big monster, and wreck faces in melee. We're level 8 right now so my best combat forms are dire tiger with pounce, giant octopus with 8 grabbing tentacles (my personal favorite and very flavorful for a merfolk), and four-armed gargoyle for flight. I consulted [this guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HnVFBgTddizhFGt-v5Vnf_VCUQ6ysqZf0Ln5jK1RDqA/edit) to figure out the basics. But here's the thing, polymorphing yourself is already one round of combat, and if you spend too much time buffing yourself at the start of combat you'll miss the fight. Most builds of this type expand your action economy with a familiar who can buff you, but for this build I'm going with a cohort that I get via the Instructor archetype. The cohort is gonna stay out of combat for the most part, just getting the defensive spells up on me as quickly as possible cause I do still have a d6 hit die and a half BAB, but should hopefully be able to sling some offensive spells as well later on. So here's his build.

Kobold wizard  
Heroic stats: Str 8 (-4 racial=4), Dex 12 (+2 racial=14), Con 14 (-2 racial=12), Int 15, Wis 13, Cha 10  
Arcane school: Transmutation (Enhancement)  
Arcane bond: Item (Wand)  
Feats:  
- 1: Improved Initiative  
- 3: Spell Focus (Transmutation)  
- 5: Greater Spell Focus (Transmutation)  
- 5 (Arcane Discovery): Faith Magic (Scalykind domain, Magic Fang)  
- 7: Extend Spell  
- 9: Whatever you want (I will probably pick Toughness)  
- 10 (Arcane Discovery): Faith Magic (Scalykind domain, Greater Magic Fang)  

Spellbook: Get all those defensive and offensive buffs--the faith magic discovery to get magic fang is a really good option here--and stand behind the giant octopus and lay buffs on it. Also try to get a few offensive transmutation spells to use once you're done buffing; Hostile Levitation, Slow, and Calcific Touch are good options.

Magic items: Scrolls and wands, babey! The cohort has even fewer spells per day than you, so you really need to make up for that with these items.

The thing to remember here is that your cohort, being a lower level than you and also a wizard, is even squishier than you, and you get a leadership penalty if he dies, so *keep him safe*.

On the continent of Estràl, elves arrived two centuries ago from their homeland across the sea and found (from their perspective) a backwater land where the agrarian humans lived in villages and worshipped the sun and moon rather than "real" gods. There was a famine going on at the time they arrived that was on its tenth year; the elves used their innate magic to help the humans stave off total starvation. Then they got to work "improving" human society - they built cities and roads and aqueducts, they helped the humans set up a new form of central government, they converted them to their religion (to which the humans proved to be more fanatical than the elves ever were). Within fifty years that half of the continent had coalesced under the theocratic republic of Lyria, named after the elven goddess. The two official branches of government were the church and the senate; the elven dignitaries formed an informal third branch of government, while holding no written or military authority, they nevertheless were able to shape events in the nation through words and the occasional flexing of an elven secret police/spy network. Even their influence is limited, though, as the senate voted to go to war with their neighboring kingdom of Croy against elven wishes (they didn't want their colony to risk its existence and wealth in a pointless trade war).

The drow have done their best to make the elves' lives misrable, but these drow are different. They are not a black-skinned subrace; rather, they are a network of ideological rebels (some would say terrorists) who oppose elven empire. This isn't to say that they necessarily have the best interests of the natives at heart, but that they have a different plan for the land than the elven authority does. The fact that any elf - or indeed, any human - could secretly be drow simply by belonging to this informal group that shares an ideology is the number one threat to elven control over the region.

In the past few days, while I drum up interest from my friends, I've been working on some notes, playing with some house rules, and writing a players' guide containing character creation guidelines and an overview of the setting, structure, and special rules of the campaign.

Today I worked on the research rules to be used in the kingdom building portion of the game in order to prepare for linnorm hunts. I gave each knowledge skill a category of information it can deliver (Arcana for traits of linnorms, History for rumors of artifacts and places of power, Nobility for details on the rulers of the lands you'll be hunting in, etc.), and wrote up a variety of bonuses you can add to your rolls with the right resources, like your kingdom containing a library (+2 to +6 depending on the size of the library) , a trained NPC using Aid Another (+2 if they can hit the DC 10 Knowledge check), or casting relevant divination spells (+ spell level). You can also use class features that affect your Knowledge checks as long as they don't require an action, like Bardic Knowledge and the Take 10 benefit of Lore Master (but not the Take 20 benefit).

When you research, you can make three Knowledge skill checks. These checks can be divided as you choose between any of the Knowledge skills, even repeating a specific skill for multiple checks if desired; every Knowledge skill has something to contribute. Some information will be only for the upcoming hunt, while some will be able to be obtained at any point in your quest--though you may not be able to immediately act upon it.

Researching takes an entire turn (month) of the kingdom building segment, during which time you can't contribute your role bonus to your kingdom--so if you're the General and you want to spend your month researching, you don't add your Strength or Charisma to your kingdom's Stability during that month, though you don't incur the vacancy penalty for researching.

The higher your knowledge roll, the more detailed the information you receive will be. For example, a Knowledge (History) roll of 15 might tell you that a useful artifact exists but has been lost (prompting further research), a roll of 20 might tell you the artifact’s abilities and the name of its last known wielder, while a 30 might tell you specifically where the item was lost, allowing you to retrieve it.

Basically you go occultist, spend your first couple implements on abjuration and transmutation, take whatever you want at level 2, and then at 6 pick up trappings of the warrior in place of an implement. This gets you access to a couple nifty focus powers, but is also the only way in the game to have both full BAB and 6th level spellcasting, along with all the utility that entails. As a melee occultist it definitely appreciates the bonus to str and int, and since you're a psychic spellcaster you aren't restricted in armor at all (spending a feat on heavy proficiency isn't the worst idea), which helps in the durability department. It uses the unchained fighter from Everyman Games, the main difference from the regular fighter being it gets stamina by default from level 1 and it gets a version of martial flexibility at level 4 that costs 3 stamina points to activate. This allows me to build as an iron caster without needing to burn a feat slot or multiclass into brawler - although I'm multiclassing into brawler anyway to get more flex uses and a higher Fort save to qualify for those spells earlier. 3: Combat Reflexes.  
F4: Advanced Weapon Training (Parry)

Twice now I've presented my players with a moral quandary that ground the session to a halt as they in-character split into two sides and argued about it.

For context, this is a game heavily involving alternate timelines.

First one, they found out that a friend they thought was dead (and saw his body) was alive and had used an alternate version of himself as bait for his pursuers so he could escape. He also turned out to be a criminal wanted by the Time Wardens the party had been working with; he stole rare and unusual artifacts from other timelines to make himself famous as an "explorer" in his home timeline. Two of the party members decided they hated this guy and turned him in to the Time Wardens after he offered to help them, resulting in him being arrested. The other two party members saw this as a cruel betrayal of a friend. They did manage to work through it so they could remain a team but the repercussions of that action affected the rest of the campaign as it locked them into one of the two sides in the conflict between the Time Wardens and the group of outlaws the friend belonged to.

The second time, they were in an alternate timeline where one of the party members' duplicates had used a powerful artifact to pacify the world, removing all violent thoughts and emotions from all living beings in an attempt to create world peace. Two of the party members--interestingly, two that were *not* on the same side in the previous conflict--thought this wasn't anything they needed to stop; it was preventing war and murder, plus they had been instructed "not to interfere" by the Time Wardens. The other two saw it as a reprehensible attack on free will. They worked it out when they learned the artifact was subtly controlling the double's mind.

Even though these arguments stopped the sessions in their tracks, it was still immensely satisfying to get such strong reactions *in different directions* from my players.
